utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. Mr. Ierace, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there are two issues that perhaps could be dealt with first very quickly. The first is a concern in relation to the timetable this week, and Mr. Stamp will say something in relation to that. It is a matter of particular concern, I think, to the Defence. So perhaps Mr. Piletta-Zanin...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. In fact, the Prosecution and the Defence met a minute ago and came to the conclusion that it would be possible for the witnesses who remain for this week, it would be possible for them to be heard, all of them could be heard up until -- by Thursday. Unless we could have a free day perhaps in order to get prepared. Unfortunately, on Friday, Ms. Pilipovic will not be here and it will therefore not be possible to examine other witnesses who weren't warned for this week for certain technical reasons. So if we could organise things in order to finish by tomorrow, that would allow everyone to use the time as best as possible rather than have the hearing suddenly brought to an end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am emphasising that, in general, this kind of arrangement would not bind the Chamber. Every day lost in court is lost in court. But Under these specific circumstances and also knowing that a witness had to arrive on Thursday or Friday, that if there was a risk that we couldn't finish with that witness, he would be here and for the whole next week we will not be sitting. Apart from that, I can't imagine that we had Good Friday off, and I wish everyone a good Easter weekend but there is another Easter weekend coming. But under these specific circumstances, the Chamber is willing to accept these proposals of the parties and only wishes that three days for three witnesses reduced to two days for three witnesses would be an encouraging experience for the parties. So, we were informed already about this plan. So please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The second issue concerns the application by the Defence for a certificate pursuant to Rule 73(C) of the Rules. That was filed on the 18th of April, being the same date -- being the date also of the decision in respect of which this certificate is sought. My question is simply whether the -- whether you, Mr. President and Your Honours, require a response from the Prosecution in relation to that application for a certificate or whether that is not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we are in a -- we are in a bit of an odd situation where we might have to deal with transitional law, that is, that it would not surprise me if one of these days a change in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence would be made public, which would require the Trial Chamber itself to grant the certificate. So we are a bit in a situation. It is, finally, it is a three members Bench of the Appeals Chamber have to deal with it. So it would be difficult for me to say what we would expect, because we will not hear that application unless the Bench of the Appeals Chamber might not have dealt with it in due time and then, of course, also depending on whether the transitional law would require the Appeals Chamber to finish that application or that, meanwhile, it would have to be dealt with by the Trial Chamber. So I saw it was about the acts and the conduct of the accused, that was the main issue. I would say that it is an issue that might have come up already in the Milosevic case, but there was no appeal lodged in that case as far as I am aware of. So let me just confer with my colleagues and see whether we, at this moment, this Chamber requires the Prosecution to respond or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is another factor and that is the Prosecution has made a further filing in relation to the decision of the 18th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have seen that. There has been a misunderstanding about a witness still to be called on an event which occurred on the same day as another event. We will deal with that rather quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will further guide you after the break, Mr. Ierace. If there is nothing else --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Nothing else, Mr. President. Might I be excused until after the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Your next witness, Mr. Aganovic, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Aganovic, I presume. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Aganovic, before giving testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth, and the text of this declaration will be handed out to you now by the usher. May I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Being called by a witness by the Prosecution, you will first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Stamp, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Stamp:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Aganovic.

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you start by telling us whether you live in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter can't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I would ask you to come forward closer to the microphones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question is, do you live in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for how long have you lived there?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Since 1964. From 1964 up until now. For 30 years, over 30 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which area of Sarajevo did you live in in 1994?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Near Rajlovac. Brijesce, Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I am asking you about the year 1994, where did you live in that year?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: In Brijesce, next to Rajlovac. It is on the outskirts of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Now, do you remember the 22nd of January, 1994?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that I was going into field. I lived in the field from 1964. I was in the field for about 15 years in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now I wish to take you to a particular day and that day is the 22nd of January, 1994.

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall that day?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That morning, did you go anywhere in particular, that is the morning of the 24th of January, 1994?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The 22nd.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, the 22nd of January, 1994. That is the day that we are going to be speaking about. That morning, did you go anywhere?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: I went to the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go there from? In other words, from where did you leave to go to the civil protection?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: From my street, Bosanska 4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what Bosanska 4 was called in 1994?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: The Klara Zetkin Street, that is what it used to be called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "from my street," you mean you lived there?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Klara Zetkin Street, as it was called then, is in Alipasino Polje district?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I take it then in 1994, at least in January 1994, you lived in Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you return home from the civil protection?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. During lunch, before lunch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About what time did you return home?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: That was in the afternoon, 1.00, half past 1.00, something like that. I can't remember exactly what time it was, but it was about midday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe the building in which you lived at Klara Zetkin 4?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: I can describe it. What do you mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a single-storey building? We can start with that.

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: It has 16 floors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in which floor did you live?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 14th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you said you went home, you went to your home on the 14th floor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you entered your building that afternoon, did you see anyone in particular outside of the building?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Not in front of the building, but the children who were killed, they were a little further away, a little further away from the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just tell us where they were and what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: They were sleighing. The weather was fine. It was silent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And exactly where were they sleighing?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, from my entrance, if you are looking towards my side -- if you are looking to my side, it was sort of north of the entrance. That's where the children would gather. It was in front of the school in Alipasino.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while you were in your apartment, did you hear anything?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Not until the first shell landed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard a shell land. I am going to ask you to describe very slowly what you heard and saw while you were in your apartment.

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I heard a hissing of the shell, as usual. That was usual. If it went over my entrance, my building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think that in the transcript part of what the witness said was not mentioned, but he is just saying what he started saying a minute ago so we could let him continue. It is just a matter of the identity of the two transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is not in the French transcript, do I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it is in the French transcript, but as it is not in the English transcript, Mr. President, it was in order to ensure that the two transcripts are identical. I think that is important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since you mention it now, I take it that it will properly be taken care of while working on the transcript. Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you heard the hissing sound of the shell passing over your apartment?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you hear anything after that?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard an explosion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did this explosion come from, the sound come from?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: From the west.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you say which particular place the shell exploded?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: It exploded above the square, over my building and then above the square, and it went down to the end of Klara Zetkin, right to the end. It passed the square where the civilian protection is. It didn't fall on the square but further beyond, towards the east. The west and east.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Could you say where in relation to your apartment building the first shell that you heard fell?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: The first shell, I didn't see where the fell, it exploded, but it was nearby. The explosion was very loud so it was possible to hear it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it behind, to the front, or to the side of the apartment building that you lived in?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Behind. Beyond my building, towards the east, the west and the east.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you heard the shell explode, what followed after that?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing. I continued to have my lunch as I knew that it hadn't hit the Solidarity Square where the civil protection was. Otherwise, I would have had to go out immediately and run to save the wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear anything after that?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: After that, a minute and-a-half or two minutes after that, a second shell fell. I didn't hear it sound, but it fell in the direction of the north, to the northern side of my entrance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the place where it fell?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see where exactly it fell, but I am sure that it fell on my -- towards my -- to my right side, to what is the north. We are situated on a slope, on a hill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say, "it fell on your right side," is that the right side Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. facing away from the front of your apartment or facing the front of your apartment?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, facing the front of my apartment. Facing the front part of my apartment, but looking from the entrance to my building, it would be the north, that is, to the right. Looking from the west where it had come from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you heard this second shell explode, did you do anything?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: I went out. I opened the window. I wanted to see whether anyone was wounded in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which window did you open?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: I opened the window of the large room, of the living room facing the west.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that a window to the front or the side or the back of your apartment?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: It is at the front side facing the west.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen --

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Where the shells were coming from. As soon as I opened the window, a third one fell right in front of my entrance so I couldn't do anything. I just heard the explosion and I was thrown back towards the window. And I ran down the stairs and, as I said, I lived on the 14th floor, and went down to the entrance of the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went down to the entrance of the building, tell us what, if anything, you saw there.

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: I saw Nermin Rizvanovic in the doorway of the entrance. He was outside at the time the detonation happened. He was about 13 years of age. I didn't see anything in particular on him, but he all of a sudden fell down on the floor and died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where he lived?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: One -- rather, two floors above me on the 16th floor. I live on the 14th and he lived on the 16th floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice anything at all about him? Was he injured?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see anyone else at the front of your apartment?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: I saw a small boy by the name of Subasic who was even younger than this one. There were no particular signs on him indicating that he was wounded, but he also died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of these children bleeding?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Not these two. Whereas other children whom I saw on the right side, that was terrible. There was blood all over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where exactly was this?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: You could see their ribs. On the right side, immediately after you leave the building, not more than 5 metres away from the entrance as you get out of the building. 5 to 10 metres. They were closer to the shell than to the entrance so they didn't manage to get to the entrance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us what, if anything, you observed about these children?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: All I was able to observe was blood and the bodies of these children scattered all around. But I was in a hurry. I was carrying these two young boys. We hoped that they would survive, but no. And that is why I didn't stay there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they, Mr. Aganovic, did the two young boys survive?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, they did not. They died on the spot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among the other children that you saw there, did you recognise any?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: I recognised these two, but I couldn't recognise others because they were covered in blood. Parts of their bodies were missing. I was not able to think much in those moments. I was trying to save these two boys.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did other residents of the building come down to help?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: There were two of them. I think the father of one of the boys who was killed and another person who had two daughters amongst this group of children who came down and covered them with a blanket. It was such a terrible sight. He didn't want it to be seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were there any wounded children there?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were. But I didn't see them. Six of the children were killed, six of them were dead, and there were some who were wounded, who were a little further from the point of impact. This is at least what I heard later on from other residents of the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from what you heard, were these children also taken away to hospital?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you arrived home sometime after 1.00 that afternoon. In the area in front of your building were the children were playing, did you see any type of military activity going on that afternoon?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: No, there was no activity at the time. It was quite sudden.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the second shell fell and you moved to the window to look out, did you see any soldiers or any type of military activity in the area outside of your apartment?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: It happened in a second, in a fraction of a second. As soon as I opened the window, this explosion occurred. So I couldn't see anything through the smoke and the flesh, and at that moment I was thrown back by the detonation. I didn't think much, I just ran down the stairs to see if anyone could be saved, if there were any casualties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were returning from the civil protection. At that time, did you work at the civil protection?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And after that as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where exactly was that office?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Behind my building, to the east of my building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say about how far from your building that civil protection office was?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: About 150 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it in a particular square? Could you tell us the name of the square?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Solidarnosti Square, the Solidarity Square.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that what it was called in 1994?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: It used to be called Klara Zetkin. After that it was renamed and it became Trg Nezanisnosti, Independence Square. I must admit I didn't give it much thought. I am not able to provide you with any specific details. I wasn't really interested in that until the war broke out. I never spent much time there at that square, actually. So I may be mistaken in respect of some of the details. It was only during the war that I became familiar with the area. But again, I am really not familiar with the details concerning this square.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of work did you do before the war started?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: In the construction business.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what type of work did you do during the war while you were in the civil protection?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Helping unloading the humanitarian aid, helping with the wounded, repairing damaged apartments damaged in shelling so that they could be repaired and made fit for living. Because shells were hitting apartments, streets. My apartment was also hit with a shell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That civil protection office, do you know of the personnel there performing any task on behalf of the military?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you ever seen soldiers there?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: I would see them in passing. Some of them would be wearing camouflage uniforms, but no weapons. They had no weapons. I would see them when they were going home, coming back from the front line, when they were off-duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, that afternoon, the afternoon of the 22nd of January, 1994, did police officers arrive on the scene to investigate the shelling?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did, afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you show them the sites, the impact sites?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But one could plainly see it. But I also showed them the place where the shell hit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that the area was shelled quite frequently. Could you tell us a little bit more about that? Were there any casualties that you know of in the area that you lived?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes there were casualties. In total, nine persons from my entrance were killed. There was a young man, aged 22 or 23, who got killed. The others were children, nine children. Actually, nine persons in total were killed, including this young man, and the rest were just children, under-age children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This young man, can you say when he was killed and what caused his death?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Before the six children were killed, he had been hit by a shell right in front of the entrance to the building. He was unloading firewood from a truck and taking it to his apartment. He was there with his relative or a cousin, and they were both killed. A shell hit a point right in front of them, apparently right before his feet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Having come from the west, also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say about how long before the 22nd of January, 1994 this young man was killed?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just approximate the time, about how long before that?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know that there have been casualties at this very square where the civilian protection is located. There was a mosque situated in the vicinity. People went there to pray. But the shelling was constant and there were many casualties. There were casualties in my street, both on the left and the right side of the street. But the worst massacre occurred when these six children were killed. And other incidents involved casualties as well. Some people got killed, some were only wounded. But I am not sure about the details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the shelling came from the west. Can you tell us why do you say that it came from the west?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Because where these children were killed, this is a spot where a shell could not have come from any other place. And in view of the kind of impact of the shell, it was easy to tell whether it had come from the south, south-westerly direction, or from the west. So you could tell according to the impact of the shell where it had come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. I have nothing further in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Aganovic, you will now be examined by counsel for the Defence. Ms. Pilipovic, is the Defence ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Cross-examined by Ms. Pilipovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Aganovic.

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified during the examination-in-chief that you had lived in Brijesce at Rajlovac since 1965?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Up until 1984.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you live after 1984?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Aganovic, the interpreters have difficulties in hearing you if you are too far away from the microphone. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are not used to it. I do understand that it is not easy. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no, I am not, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Aganovic, so you have lived in Bosanska since 1984; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when the conflict in Sarajevo started, according to you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When in 1992 did this conflict in Sarajevo break out?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe it was in April or May. I don't know exactly, but it must have been sometime between April and May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you respond to the call-up for mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. Actually, I did, but I was declared unfit for military service so I was assigned to the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the exact street or the exact location where the premises of the civilian protection were housed?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I couldn't describe that in detail. I must admit, I was not very interested in these things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe at least the building where the premises of the civilian protection were locate?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: The buildings in question were three or four-storey buildings, not very high.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which part of the Alipasino Polje neighbourhood was the civilian protection located?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Behind my building. Not more than 150 metres away from my building, but behind it. To the east of the entrance to my building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these buildings also part of your street?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There are some high-rise buildings in my street but the buildings surrounding the square were not that high, as I said, three or four-storey buildings. There was a skyscraper in the vicinity but these buildings were not very high.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you telling us that the civilian protection building was located at that square?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Behind your building?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether, according to your knowledge, the police also had their premises at the square near these buildings?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: The police is located a little further away from the building. It is -- it is still there and they were there even before the war and during the war and after the war. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the premises of the Croatian Defence Council were also there on the square?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: No, they were not. The Croatian Defence Council, as far as I know, never had any premises there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have lived at Alipasino Polje since 1984. I would like to know whether there was a restaurant called "Stela" near the civilian protection building?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Stela? No. No. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified today about the incident which occurred on the 22nd of January, as you stated?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The incident took place in Klara Zetkin Street at house number 4?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what is the distance between the place where the incident took place and the front lines?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Looking from my entrance towards the west, I think that they were some 2000 metres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're telling us that it was 2000 metres away from your house looking towards the westward part of Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Nedzarici, Stup and Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say Nedzarici, Stup and Ilidza. I am interested in Stup. Do you know which army had its positions there?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: There are actually two locations there, the Stupsko Brdo and Stup, and the separation line was there opposing two armies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which particular army was there?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the BH army and the other army. I mean the soldiers of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say the army or the soldiers of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it was called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as the BH army is concerned, do you know whether during that period of time during the conflict, how they were dressed?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Some had uniforms and some had civilian clothes. People managed as best as they could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the conflict in the town of Sarajevo, in the neighbourhood where you lived and with respect to Nedzarici, where exactly the positions of the BH army were?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't clearly see them. I could see the area of Nedzarici and the houses there and that is where the positions were. But the troops were even further away, some 5 kilometres from there, so I was not able to see them. I mean, I didn't see the separation line. That was at quite a distance, some 5 kilometres away, as I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you could see the area of the Nedzarici including small family houses there?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you telling us that Serbs lived in Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, only Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you telling us that the army of Republika Srpska was deployed there?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the BH army soldiers were with respect to Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: To the right, towards the north.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what specific location, what specific street or part of the town that is?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe the area in question was called Stupsko Brdo, the Stup hill. At least that is what I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When looking from your window facing Nedzarici, is it possible for you to see the area called Vojnicko Polje?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: No, you cannot see Vojnicko Polje. All I can see is Alipasino Polje. But Vojnicko Polje is further away towards the west. It is actually very close to Nedzarici. It is part of Nedzarici so I think it is some 2 or 3 kilometres away from my building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which army held its positions in Vojnicko Polje?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was the BH army, but the separation line with the Serb army was -- was there as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your window, can you see the Mojmilo hill?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. It is situated towards the south, to the left side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you leave your apartment and the entrance to your building, are you facing the Mojmilo hill?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I mean, you can see the Mojmilo hill, but the entrance to the building itself faces west.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the conflict in Sarajevo, 1992, 1993 and 1994, do you know which army had their positions at the Mojmilo hill?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Serb army was at the edge of the Mojmilo hill area, but the JNA was there before, that is the Yugoslav army, and then the Serb army. But the BH army, that is the defence, the Bosnian defence, was also there, and these people didn't wear uniforms. They wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us during the conflict in Sarajevo in 1992, 1993, and 1994, was there any fighting in Alipasino Polje between the two armies?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Mojmilo and Nedzarici and, as I said, in Vojnicko Polje, that is where there was fighting from the beginning, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say, "from the beginning of 1992," could you tell us whether there was any fighting in 1993 and 1994 between those two armies?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: No, there wasn't because the army of Republika Srpska had withdrawn from some positions and these others came up closer. So there was no fighting. It was mostly in the surroundings of Sarajevo, in the hills. There was more free territory then so that the BH army also had its positions in the hills that they got in the course of the fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that the BH army had positions which they obtained in the course of the fighting in the hills, can you tell us which parts this army was in?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was Mojmilo. It was in Mojmilo, Zuc, and Stupsko Brdo. Mojmilo, Zuc, Stupsko Brdo. That is what I knew about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Aganovic, could you tell us what the day was like on the 21st of -- 22nd of January?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: It was a fine day. It was warm. People were out to get some air because they had been spending time in the houses, in cellars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that after you heard or rather saw the third shell, that you went down?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did it take you to get to the entrance?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: I ran down and maybe it took me a minute and-a-half or so because I was running very quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that you ran up into the lift, are you telling us that the lift was working but you didn't take it?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, when there was electricity, it would work, but naturally it didn't work when there was no electricity. I didn't pay any attention to the lift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say there was no electricity --

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, sometimes there was and sometimes there wasn't. But I didn't want to -- I think the -- I don't think I should have used the lift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992, 1993 and 1994, could you tell us how often the electricity supply was cut off?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was a reduction in the electricity supply. This happened very often in the course of the day. Sometimes someone would have no electricity for a few days or for a day or for half a day. It depended. And then there would be failures so you wouldn't have any electricity again and you would wait for your turn again, because people sort of took it in turns to have a supply of electricity. They tried to save electricity. But when there was shelling, a fault would occur and it was necessary to wait again. Sometimes there was electricity, sometimes there wasn't any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Aganovic, when you say that -- when you talk about these reductions in the electricity supply, can you tell us what the situation was like in Alipasino Polje with regard to water?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was not very good. People went to sources to get water. To the "A" phase, that is below, further down below, there was a water supply there. But they would also take turns to do this. They would always go occasionally. Water wasn't available all the time. It was available occasionally. So as far as water is concerned, it was more difficult -- it was quite difficult to obtain it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Aganovic, when you say sometimes there was water and sometimes there wasn't, are you trying -- are you telling us that there was a reduction in the water supply, too?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When this incident occurred in which children were killed, could you tell us how many children died on that day?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Six children died. I don't know how many wounded children there were, but I know about these six children. There were six children in front of the entrance itself. One of the children was from another building, but I knew the other five. They were all refugees, apart from one, that is Nerman Rizvanovic. He had been a resident for some time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Aganovic, you told us the police came to the site of the incident.

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: They came later on, when the children had been taken away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us how long afterwards they came?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you that. I don't know whether they came immediately because I stayed in the civilian protection while the children were being taken away. So I can't tell you whether the commission came on that same day. I think that they came on that day because we stayed on in the civilian protection, and this is why I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that you think that the police came on the same day --

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Not the police, but a commission of some kind, and the television, they went there to film.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that occasion, did someone speak to you?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Someone asked me what had happened, how it had happened, when it had happened, where I was at the time and whom I had saved. I told them what I saw and what I was able to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You tell us -- you are telling us that six children died. If I tell you that there is a record which states, according to the commission and people who were present, that five children were killed, what would you say?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: No, six. Five from my building, but from another building -- there was another child from another building, so that was the sixth child. And in addition to them, there were wounded children to the left and to the right. They had been wounded by the shell. I didn't see them, but I heard that they had been wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are telling us that six children were killed?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it says so on the plaque which they put up there, which the city put up there. It says six children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on the basis of that information, as it says that there was six children on the plaque, it was on that basis that you tell us there was six?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, well, it says so on the plaque and it is common knowledge that there were six children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Aganovic, you told us that a school was in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not exactly in the vicinity, but maybe 200 or 300 metres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether that school worked during the conflict from 1992 to 1994?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not in the beginning but later, when people got used to the war, it was open.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us the name of that school?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: No, because I wasn't that interested in it. I didn't have any children who went to school. I didn't have such small children so that I didn't know what it was called, what its name was, and I wasn't interested in this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that a television crew came, could you tell us which channel came to film this?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Our television, from the "A" phase, below the hills, so it is very close to them. As soon as something happens, they come. They came to my flat when a shell fell and filmed there. They hear about it and after a certain time, they come to film this, when they hear that something has happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Aganovic, when my learned colleague put to you a question, you told them about an incident in which, as you say, two people died while they were carrying firewood.

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, given that you said that this was before the 22nd of January, 1994, could you tell us when this incident happened?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I can't tell you. I don't know the year or the month. I know that it was in winter and they were carrying firewood. It was cold, but I don't know what month it was. No one was interested in when it would fall and what would happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are telling us that you didn't see this incident?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw both of them. I saw the boy and his cousin. She was 13 years old and the boy was about 21, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us their names? What was the young man's name?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't -- I don't know his name. He was a refugee. They were refugees so I never spoke to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that it was winter, but could you tell us what time of day this happened?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: It was just before the evening, late afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you know whether there was any fighting in that period?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: No, there wasn't. A shell would fall unexpectedly. It was quite sudden. The shells would always fall unexpectedly. No one would ever expect such things to happen. It simply happens and that is it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Aganovic, could you tell us when this plaque was erected in Sarajevo, the one in which it says that six children died?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: In the same year, in the spring, I think. They brought the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. plaque, sort of monument, and inscribed on the plaque they said that six children had died. It was a sort of commemorative plaque on the building in front of the entrance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you lived in this building where the incident took place?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Aganovic, when you worked -- during the period you worked in the civilian protection, you said that you distributed humanitarian aid. Could you tell us how often you would distribute humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Every 15 days. Sometimes 17 or 18 days, but usually every 15 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With regard to your part of Alipasino Polje, could you tell us in which part of Alipasino Polje you would distribute humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Around my building, everyone had their own area. There were people who were -- who had the duty for doing this. I was part of this commission for distributing humanitarian aid. Everyone had his own building. Everyone had a commission and assistant, so I wasn't assigned to other buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1993 and 1994, could you tell us during which period of the day humanitarian aid would be distributed?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that depended. Sometimes around midday, sometimes in the morning. It varied. It depended on the possibilities. Whenever it was possible to load and unload aid because they would send this aid from warehouses. No specific times had been sent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were working for the civilian protection, did you have any contact with representatives of the UN and UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. They were commanders in the civilian protection. They were officials who would speak to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the incident of the 22nd of January, did you see or were you informed of the arrival of the representatives of the UN?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, sometimes they would come. They would usually come to the site, but I didn't really pay attention to this and I didn't speak to them either. It was not necessary. There were certain officials who would speak to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see members of the UN come to the site when this incident occurred, and did you see them filming?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: When I gave my statement, I know that there were members of the UN who were there. Otherwise, whenever there was a large-scale massacre, they would appear there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us when you gave a statement for the first time and whom you gave it to?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know but it was during that same week, during those same days, more or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, may I remind you that you spent as much time in cross as the Prosecution took in examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I shall try to bring my cross-examination to a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Aganovic, do you know whether there were any paramilitary units in the area in which you lived in Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: There were paramilitary units only once the war had started. Later, it was the real army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the area in which you lived, which paramilitary units were in that area?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. There weren't really paramilitary units. Well, I mean, they were, but they appeared later on because whoever could save someone or whoever had weapons would turn up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time that the conflict broke out as you said, could you tell us which units were present in Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, some called Celo, Krusko. They were called something like that. They were independent. They could defend themselves independently, to the extent that this was possible because there were weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say Celo and Krusko, could you tell us where the staffs were and were they units were located?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, this was in Stupsko Brdo, these units were there. But the army was there already, the BH army was there, and these people, they lived in flats. Nothing had really been organised, no accommodation had been organised. These people would stay in houses. There were no barracks or anything like that that they could open up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are telling us that the soldiers from those units and later on from the BH army, they stayed in private houses?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: In private houses, yes. They were just trying to determine where they would meet and what they would do, but this was not something I was interested in. This is something that I heard about. From the beginning, it was surrounded and you just ended up where you were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Aganovic, when you say that the BH army had been formed after this, do you know whether the 102 Motorised Brigade was in the area of Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: No, the 101st was there, but when they were there in the barracks, the Viktor Burban barracks, which is where the regular army of the former Yugoslavia was located, and at the time the BH army was there in Viktor Burban. It was the 101 Motorised but I don't know about any others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Aganovic, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think there is a problem in the transcript to the extent that I think that I heard the witness say that these soldiers communicated by telephone, and this is quite important in the eyes of the Defence, and this does not appear in the English transcript. I can't see it in the English transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... approximately would that have been, Mr. Piletta-Zanin

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About 30 seconds ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that is when the questions were about the Motorised Brigade, whether the 101st and 102nd. Did you say anything about telephone communication between different parts of military units or army units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't. I wasn't in contact with. No, no, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, what the witness has just said, he has said in his own language. I think that he said he wasn't in contact with them. What the witness said a minute ago was that the soldiers communicated via telephone -- no, I am sorry. I apologise. What the witness just said was that the soldiers who were in private accommodation, in a certain sense, he said that he communicated over the telephone. I think that the witness said so, and I can see in agreement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, they didn't have any premises of their own

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Aganovic, did you say anything about telephone communication between military people before, using private telephone or other telephone communications used by? Did you say anything about that? We can't hear you in your own language, you see, so we are dependent on the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin says he heard you saying something about it. It was not translated. Did you say anything about such a subject?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat what you said, exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that from the beginning, from the very beginning, these soldiers who were mounting a resistance who were in that war, they didn't have any barracks in which they could meet. They would come to agreements from the houses in which they were. They would agree on where they would meet. That's how -- that's what happened. There was no other way. Some would be in one building, some were in other buildings. So I assume that this is how they would try to agree where they would meet. There was no other way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you say that you take it that they communicated by telephone in order to make the arrangements for meeting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know that they used the telephone or do you assume that they used the telephone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that they used a telephone because they were dispersed throughout the town because there was -- there weren't any barracks where they could meet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, for your assistance because it really seems to have fallen away specific part of the testimony, and as you know, the Chamber is always -- is always happy to hear about these things that might create confusion. Mr. Stamp, is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions, and it will be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, very brief. Please proceed. Re-examined by Mr. Stamp:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the Viktor Burban barracks were located?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Also behind my building, to the east. Some three kilometres away from my building, 3.000 metres way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that soldiers stayed in private houses sometimes.

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: They were no soldiers, properly speaking. Most of them were wearing civilian clothes. They were not a real army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. What I want to find out, if the building that you lived in had any groups of soldiers residing there.

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: There were no groups of soldiers anywhere. There could have been a soldier or two living at one particular house number. The building had several entrances, and they met as best as they could. They tried to call each other by telephone and to arrange where they would meet, and so on and so forth, but I wasn't much interested in that because I was a member of the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of any soldiers being at the barracks of any building -- of there being any barracks for soldiers in the area that you lived in?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: No. There was no barracks at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: They lived in their private flats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is all, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Judge El Mahdi has one or more questions to you, Mr. Aganovic. Questioned by the Court: JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Mr. Aganovic, you stated that at the beginning there was no army, properly speaking, so there must have been groups which organised themselves as best as they could in order to mount a defence. What date did you have in mind when you said that this change -- when do you think that the army was established? When were the barracks, the headquarters, and everything else necessary for an army, established? Was it in 1992? 1993? 1994?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Beginning of 1994, end of 1993, beginning of 1994. It was during that period of time that the barracks were being taken over from the JNA. There was no Serb army at the time, but only the JNA which was withdrawing at the time pursuant to an agreement. So the Bosnian defenders could take up quarters in their barracks. So they were no longer located in various flats around the town, but in the barracks. And as far as I know, there were three such barracks that had been handed over to this Bosnian army. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] So you are talking about 1994, the time when this accident occurred?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it had already happened, even before that this transfer of the army. I don't know exactly when it happened. I know that the former Yugoslav army, the JNA, left the barracks at one point in time and then the barracks were taken up by this other army. There was no conflict. It was all done with an accordance with an agreement, that is that the barracks should be liberated, but I don't know exactly when. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] An agreement between whom?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Between the Yugoslav army and the command of our army, I mean, the one that was in Sarajevo, including the Presidency. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And this had taken place before January 1994?

utterances.speaker: REFIK AGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, before. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Aganovic, since I have no questions to you, this concludes your testimony in this Court. You will understand that it is important for this Chamber to hear the answer of witnesses to questions both of the Prosecution and the Defence and, of course, also the questions of the Bench. I would like to thank you very much for having come to The Hague. We all know it is a far distance, and I thank you for giving answers to all these questions. I hope that you have a safe journey home again. Thank you very much for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn until five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 11.12 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before the Prosecution calls its next witness, may I just ask, Mr. Ierace - this morning my computer was not connected - could you please clarify exactly what you meant by whether the Prosecution in relation to the application for a certificate for an interlocutory appeal, whether that was necessary or not. Was that in whatever way related to the corrigendum you might expect or was it just in general?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Separate from the corrigendum, Mr. President. The Defence has sought a certificate pursuant to Rule 73(C). The Rule does not mention whether the Prosecution has the opportunity to assist the Trial Chamber by making a response to the application for a certificate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it is the Trial Chamber who does so?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me have a look. It is an interlocutory appeal Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and that is -- let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It is a preliminary step.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is 73(D), says: "Decisions on all other motions or the Trial Chamber may certify that -- " You are referring to 73(C). Yes, I do agree with you. It is a decision involving evidence and procedure. It is not a decision on a motion. It is a request, not a motion. If you would have called it a motion, then even we would have to discuss whether it was under 73(C) or (D). But I do understand what you mean. Well, I mean, filing, in my view, is not necessary, but if you could give -- I mean, if there is any specific response you would like to make. If you say, "We agree it should be the Trial Chamber that deals with the question of what are the acts and the conducts of the accused," then I don't think it is necessary that you could express yourself orally and we would know at least what the position of the Prosecution is. If, on the other hand, the Prosecution would go in a lot of detail on the matter itself already and say, well, this is now of some importance for the case law of the Tribunal or whatever, if we have the whole story, we would rather read it. If you say, "Well, our position is quite clear. We do agree," or "We not agree," then it could be done early as well. It makes it possible for us to give a quicker response to the request.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps tomorrow morning, if that is convenient, I could indicate very briefly what our position is in order to save time, if that would assist you, rather than do a lengthy written response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the issue is such, it will either be dealt with by the Appeal Chamber or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: But in relation to the issuing of the certificate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is just preliminary matter. Of course, it is in relation with the problem raised by the Defence, the issue raised by the Defence in its application for certificate. I leave it up to you. If we get a long story -- one of the problems, of course, is the Chamber will not be sitting and some members of the -- some Judges of this Chamber will not be present during next week. So if we could deal with it on short notice, that would be preferable.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, just to be clear on that, would it be acceptable if we indicated tomorrow morning early in relation to the issuance of the certificate? If you think there is no need for that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the Chamber would like to know the position of the Prosecution, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you. Might I be excused again, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I think that you noted that the Defence was extremely concise in the paper that it presented to you. We did not address the details in order to know whether our Rule 92 bis was applicable or not. So we place the debate on this terrain, and it is true that we still have to respond. Whether -- if we are talking about whether the certificate has to be given or not, then I think at this point the Defence will not have to make any response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course we cannot give any other decision, but as far as I understand, the Defence wants the issue of what is act and conduct of the accused, and 92 bis (A) is to be decided by the Appeals Chamber. I think that is the main issue, as far as I see it. Yes, okay. That's clear. Then, Mr. Ierace, you are excused. I think we had still one or -- did you receive already the newly translated copy of Exhibit -- Madam Registrar, could you please assist. Did you give it already to me? No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As we discussed last Monday Exhibit 1675, with its new translation, which makes it .2, was provided to the Defence. Is there any -- and since the Exhibit itself, 1675, was not tendered yet, we finally concluded that the Prosecution was tendering 1675 and 1675.2. Is there any additional observation to be made, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, I can see "167," "165," "1675" -- no, it is okay now. The transcript has just changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, as soon as the right number appears, you better say that the last numbers are the correct ones, because if you repeat the numbers, there is always the risk that they will be distorted again. Is there any other observation to be made in respect of this translation? You have seen it by now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether we have received it -- yes, yes, we have undoubtedly received it. No, no other remarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then 1675 and 1675.2 are admitted into evidence. Mr. Stamp, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness, which I do understand is Eldar Hafizovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We are, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you hear me in a language you understand? May I ask you to speak your answers loud so that the interpreters can also hear you. Mr. Hafizovic, I presume, before giving testimony in this court, the Rules require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. And the text of that declaration will be handed out to you now by the usher, and may I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Hafizovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The order in this Court is you will first be examined by the party who called you, that is the Prosecution, and then you will be examined by the Defence, and if the Judges have any questions to you, they will put them to you as well. Mr. Stamp, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President Examined by Mr. Stamp:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you start by telling us your full name?

utterances.speaker: ELDAR HAFIZOVIC
utterances.text: Eldar Hafizovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you work, sir?

utterances.speaker: ELDAR HAFIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of work do you do?

utterances.speaker: ELDAR HAFIZOVIC
utterances.text: I am employed at the Videx audio company, and I am in charge of adjusting the hearing devices that are used by the people with hearing problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you live in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ELDAR HAFIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long have you lived there?

utterances.speaker: ELDAR HAFIZOVIC
utterances.text: Since my birth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall the conflict in Sarajevo between 1992 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: ELDAR HAFIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When that conflict started, where were you living in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ELDAR HAFIZOVIC
utterances.text: I was living at Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you begin to live at Dobrinja? How did you come to start living at Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: ELDAR HAFIZOVIC
utterances.text: My parents are divorced. I was living with my mother at Nerkiza Smajlovica number 7 in the Alipasino neighbourhood. That was my address. So I went to visit my father, who lived at Dobrinja, and that is where the war found me. Dobrinja was cut off from the rest of the city and I was no longer able to go back to the town of Sarajevo, and that is how I remained in Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About when was it that you started to live in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: ELDAR HAFIZOVIC
utterances.text: Ever since the beginning of the war. I left for Dobrinja on the 1st of May, that was the Bajram, our religious holiday, and I stayed on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This would be the 1st of May, 1992, I take it?

utterances.speaker: ELDAR HAFIZOVIC
utterances.text: No. Actually, I am not sure about the date. Maybe it is not the 1st May precisely. But, anyway, it was a holiday, and I went to see my father for the holiday and I stayed in Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it in 1992, though?

utterances.speaker: ELDAR HAFIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you go there to see your father alone or did you go with any other relative?

utterances.speaker: ELDAR HAFIZOVIC
utterances.text: I went to visit him with my brother who is younger than me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you remain in Dobrinja for the duration of the war?

utterances.speaker: ELDAR HAFIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall -- well, before we get to that. Did you live at one place in Dobrinja or at more than one place while you were there?

utterances.speaker: ELDAR HAFIZOVIC
utterances.text: I lived at several places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you move from place to place?

utterances.speaker: ELDAR HAFIZOVIC
utterances.text: I was wounded several times. My apartment, that is where I was living at the time, was hit on several occasions and quite a few apartments were damaged and that is the reason why I had to move to another flat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I take you to the 4th of February, 1994 and speak about that day. Where were you living on that day?

utterances.speaker: ELDAR HAFIZOVIC
utterances.text: I was living at number 5 in Oslobodilaca Sarajeva in Dobrinja 1 neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oslobodilaca Sarajeva is the name of the street and the building number is number 5; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELDAR HAFIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the house number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of house is it? Could you just briefly describe it to us?

utterances.speaker: ELDAR HAFIZOVIC
utterances.text: It is a residential building consisting of several entrances, several house numbers, and I lived at number 5.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it is a one-storey building or does it have many different storeys?

utterances.speaker: ELDAR HAFIZOVIC
utterances.text: It has several storeys.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which storey did you live on?

utterances.speaker: ELDAR HAFIZOVIC
utterances.text: I lived on the third floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the street Oslobodilaca Sarajeva was at the front of the building; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ELDAR HAFIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us what is to the back of the building?

utterances.speaker: ELDAR HAFIZOVIC
utterances.text: There is a playground behind the building, on the back side of the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what is the surface of this playground at the back of the building made of?

utterances.speaker: ELDAR HAFIZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but 15 to 20 metres at the most, maybe -- maybe 50 metres. The length may have been about 50 metres and the width more or less the same, that is the entire area where the park is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the playground in that park, does it have an asphalt surface?

utterances.speaker: ELDAR HAFIZOVIC
utterances.text: Part of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was your brother, your younger brother, living on the 4th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: ELDAR HAFIZOVIC
utterances.text: At the same address with me, with my grandmother and with my grandfather.
